title: Process Automation and Logic
summary: Make Salesforce do the work: flows, clean Apex, safe queries and triggers that handle 200 records as easily as one.

lessons.title: Flow and approvals: automation with clicks
lessons.objective: Identify the capabilities of the declarative process automation features.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Declarative automation** means making Salesforce do work with clicks, not code. You build it in Setup. The main tool today is **Flow**. A flow can update records, send emails, ask users questions and run on a schedule. An **approval process** sends a record to people who say yes or no.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A smart kitchen. A flow is a recipe the kitchen follows by itself when something happens: milk runs low, so add milk to the list. An approval is asking a parent before a big purchase. Where it stops: some jobs are too complex for a recipe card, and those still need Apex.

cards.title: The flow types
items: **Screen flow**: shows screens and guides a user step by step.
**Record-triggered flow**: runs when a record is created, updated or deleted.
**Schedule-triggered flow**: runs at a set time for a batch of records.
**Platform event-triggered flow**: runs when a platform event message arrives.
**Autolaunched flow**: no trigger. Apex, another flow or the REST API starts it.

cards.title: Before or after the save
cards.body: A record-triggered flow picks when it runs. **Fast Field Updates** run before the save. They can change only the record that started the flow, so they're very fast. **Actions and Related Records** run after the save. They can create, update or delete other records, send emails and call Apex.

cards.title: Paths that wait
cards.body: After-save flows can add more paths. A **scheduled path** runs later, like 3 days before the Close Date. A path that runs **asynchronously** runs right after the save is committed, in its own transaction.

cards.title: Approval processes
cards.body: An **approval process** has entry criteria, approval steps and actions. Actions can run on submit, approve, reject or recall. They can update fields, send emails or create tasks. By default, the record is **locked** while it waits, so only approvers and admins can edit it.

**Workflow rules** and **Process Builder** are legacy tools. Salesforce says to build new automation in Flow. If an answer suggests a new workflow rule or process, it's usually wrong. They still show up in the order of execution, because old ones can still run.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Before = fast, same record. After = actions, other records.** Screens need a user. Schedules need a clock. Events need a message.

terms.say: Making Salesforce do work by itself using setup screens and clicks, instead of writing code.
Salesforce's main click-based automation tool. You drag steps onto a canvas and connect them, like a flowchart that really runs.
A set path that sends a record to people to approve or reject, like asking your boss to sign a form.
A flow with screens a person clicks through, like a step-by-step form or wizard.
A flow that starts by itself when a record is created, updated or deleted.
A flow with no screens and no trigger of its own. Something else starts it, like Apex or another flow.
The before-save choice for a record-triggered flow. It only changes the record being saved, so it's very quick.
The after-save choice for a record-triggered flow. It can touch other records, send emails and call Apex.
A part of an after-save flow that waits and runs later, at a time based on the record, like 3 days before a date.
An old click tool for automation. Salesforce now says to use Flow instead, but old processes can still run.

lessons.title: Variables, constants and data types
lessons.objective: Understand how to declare variables, constants, methods, modifiers, Apex interfaces, and the appropriate use cases for each.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **variable** is a named box that holds a value. In Apex, every variable has a **data type**, like `Integer`, `String` or `Account`. The type says what can go in the box. A **constant** is a box you fill once and never change.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Labeled jars in a kitchen. The sugar jar only takes sugar, just like an `Integer` only takes whole numbers. A constant is a jar with the lid glued on. Where it stops: an Apex jar you never filled isn't empty. It holds `null`.

cards.title: Common data types
items: **Primitives**: `Integer`, `Long`, `Decimal`, `Double`, `String`, `Boolean`, `Date`, `Datetime`, `Id`.
**sObjects**: one record, like `Account` or `Invoice__c`.
**Collections**: `List` (ordered, repeats allowed), `Set` (no repeats), `Map` (key to value).
**Enums**: a fixed list of named values.

cards.title: Declaring variables
cards.body: Write the type, then the name. A variable you don't set starts as `null`. That's true even for an `Integer` or a `Boolean`.

cards.title: Constants
cards.body: `final` means it can be set only once. A `static final` variable is a class-wide constant. Set it where you declare it, or in a `static` block.

cards.title: Static or instance
cards.body: A **static** variable belongs to the class, not to one object. All code in the same **transaction** shares one copy, and it resets when the transaction ends. An **instance** variable belongs to each object you make with `new`.

cards.title: A String quirk
cards.body: `==` on Strings **ignores case**, so `'abc' == 'ABC'` is true. Use `equals()` when case matters. But `Map` keys and `switch` values of type `String` do care about case.
Apex `static` is not shared across users or requests. It lives for one transaction only. So a static counter can't count logins across the org. It starts fresh in every transaction.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Type, name, value.** No value means `null`. `final` means set once. `static final` means one constant for the whole class.

terms.say: A named box in your code that holds a value, like a number or a name. You can read it and change it.
The kind of value a box can hold: a whole number, text, a date, a record and so on.
A value that is set once and then can never change, like the number of days in a week.
The simple, built-in kinds of values: numbers, text, true or false, dates and Ids.
A Salesforce record held in Apex, like one Account or one Contact, with its fields.
Boxes that hold many values at once. Apex has three kinds: List, Set and Map.
Means "no value at all". It isn't zero and it isn't empty text. It's nothing.
A keyword that means "this can be set only once". After that, the value is locked.
Belongs to the class itself, not to one object. Everyone in the same transaction shares one copy.
Everything that happens in one request, start to finish. It all saves together, or it is all undone together.

lessons.title: Methods, access modifiers and interfaces
lessons.objective: Understand how to declare variables, constants, methods, modifiers, Apex interfaces, and the appropriate use cases for each.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **method** is a named set of steps your code can call, like `calculateTax()`. An **access modifier** says who may call a method or see a variable. An **interface** is a promise: any class that signs it must have certain methods.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Rooms in a house. `private` is your bedroom: only you. `public` is the living room: the whole family, meaning your app. `global` is the front porch: anyone, even neighbors, meaning other apps and APIs. Where it stops: `protected` is odd. It's for inner classes and subclasses only.

cards.title: The four access modifiers
items: `private`: only inside this class. It's **the default** when you write nothing.
`protected`: this class, its inner classes and classes that extend it. Instance members only.
`public`: any Apex in the same app or namespace.
`global`: any Apex anywhere, plus SOAP API. The class must be `global` too.

cards.title: Parts of a method
cards.body: Access modifier, optional `static`, then the **return type** (`void` means it returns nothing), the name and the parameters. Call a `static` method on the class name, like `TaxUtil.addTax(100)`.

cards.title: An interface and a class that signs it
cards.body: The interface lists methods with no body. The class uses `implements` and must define **every** method in it.

cards.title: virtual and abstract
cards.body: A `virtual` class can be extended, and its `virtual` methods can be replaced with `override`. An `abstract` class can't be created with `new`. Its `abstract` methods have no body, and subclasses must fill them in. Without one of these keywords, a class **can't be extended**.

Apex `public` is **not** Java's `public`. It means "same namespace or package". To reach code from outside the package, or from SOAP API, you need `global`. And with no modifier at all, a method is `private`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Me, family, team, world**: `private`, `protected`, `public`, `global`. An interface is a promise: sign it with `implements`, then keep every part.

terms.say: A named list of steps in a class that you can run by calling its name, like pressing a button.
A word in front of a method or variable that says who is allowed to use it.
A promise that lists methods by name. Any class that signs it must write all those methods.
Only code inside the same class can use it. This is what you get if you write no modifier.
The class, its inner classes and the classes that extend it can use it. Nobody else can.
Any Apex in the same app or namespace can use it. In Apex it does not mean the whole world.
Any Apex anywhere can use it, even other packages and the SOAP API. Use it rarely.
The kind of value a method hands back when it finishes. `void` means it hands back nothing.
The word a class uses to sign an interface's promise. Then it must write every listed method.
A class or method that is only an outline. You can't create the class with `new`; a subclass fills it in.

lessons.title: Control flow: if, loops and switch
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, assess how Apex control flow statements will execute and when to apply different control flow statements.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Control flow** decides which lines run, and how many times. `if` and `else` pick a path. **Loops** repeat work. `switch` picks one branch from many values. `break` jumps out of a loop, and `continue` skips to its next turn.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A board game. `if` is a fork in the path. A loop is going around the board again. `switch` is a spinner that lands on one color. `break` is leaving the game early. `continue` is skipping just this turn. Where it stops: an Apex `switch` never falls through to the next branch.

cards.title: Loops
cards.code:
for (Integer i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }           // counter loop
for (Account a : accts) { }                   // list or set loop
for (Account a : [SELECT Id FROM Account]) { } // SOQL for loop
while (n > 0) { n--; }                        // checks first
do { n--; } while (n > 0);                    // runs at least once
cards.body: A `do-while` loop always runs once before it checks. A `while` loop may run zero times.

cards.title: switch
cards.body: `switch on` works with `Integer`, `Long`, `String`, `sObject` and `Enum`. At most one `when` runs. `when else` is optional, and it must come last.

cards.title: Short forms
cards.body: The **ternary operator** is a tiny if/else on one line: `qty > 100 ? 'Big' : 'Small'`. The **safe navigation operator** `?.` returns `null` instead of throwing an error when the left side is null.

cards.title: SOQL for loop
cards.body: A **SOQL for loop** gets query results in chunks of **200**. Use it when a query could return many rows, so they don't all sit in memory at once. It still counts as one query.

A `switch` on a `String` **cares about case**, but `==` on Strings doesn't. `when 'hot'` won't match `'Hot'`. Also, you never need `break` inside a `when` block. Apex never runs the next block by accident.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **If picks. Loops repeat. Switch spins once.** `break` leaves the loop. `continue` skips one turn. `do-while` always runs at least once.

terms.say: The rules that decide which lines of code run next, and how many times they run.
Code that repeats the same steps, again and again, until a condition says stop.
Jumps right out of a loop. The loop stops, and the code after it runs.
Skips the rest of this turn of the loop and goes on to the next turn.
Checks one value and runs the one block that matches it, like a spinner landing on a color.
The catch-all block in a switch. It runs when no other value matched. It must come last.
A loop that runs its steps first and checks the condition after. So it always runs at least once.
A one-line if/else: a question, then the value if yes, then the value if no.
The `?.` sign. If the thing on its left is null, you get null back instead of a crash.
A loop written right around a query. It fetches records in chunks of 200, which saves memory.

lessons.title: SOQL and SOSL in Apex
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, write SOSL, SOQL, and DML statements in Apex, and assess what they will return.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **SOQL** asks the database for records of one object and its related objects, like "all open Cases for this Account". **SOSL** searches for words across many objects at once, like a search box. In Apex you write both inside square brackets.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: SOQL is asking a librarian for every book on shelf B by one author. You know where to look. SOSL is typing a word into the library's search bar and getting books, magazines and DVDs back. Where it stops: both have hard limits on how much they return.

cards.title: SOQL in Apex
cards.body: `:region` is a **bind variable**: an Apex value used in the query. It also blocks SOQL injection. The inner query is a **child subquery** that uses the relationship name `Contacts`.

cards.title: Parents and children
cards.body: Go up to a parent with a dot: `SELECT Name, Account.Name FROM Contact`. Custom relationships use `__r`, like `Invoice__r.Total__c`. Go down to children with a subquery.

cards.title: SOSL in Apex
cards.body: SOSL returns a **list of lists**, one inner list per object, in `RETURNING` order. `FIND` is required. Search ignores case and allows wildcards like `*`.

cards.title: Limits to know (per transaction)
items: **100** SOQL queries (200 in async Apex).
**50,000** rows returned by SOQL in total.
**20** SOSL queries, and **2,000** rows per SOSL query.

cards.title: User mode
cards.body: Add `WITH USER_MODE` to make a query respect the running user's object, field and record access. `WITH SYSTEM_MODE` skips those checks. Choose one on purpose instead of trusting defaults.

Putting a query into a single record throws a `QueryException` if it finds **zero rows** or **more than one**. Putting it into a `List` just gives an empty list. "It returns `null`" is the classic wrong answer.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **SOQL: one object family, and you know where. SOSL: one word, many objects.** One row into one record? Be sure exactly one comes back.

terms.say: Salesforce's query language. It asks for records of one object, and its parents or children, that match your filters.
Salesforce's search language. It looks for a word or phrase across many objects at once.
An Apex value put into a query with a colon, like `:region`. It's safe, so users can't sneak code into the query.
A small query inside a bigger one that brings back each record's children, like an Account's Contacts.
The ending used to follow a custom relationship in a query, like `Invoice__r.Total__c` to reach a parent's field.
What SOSL gives back: one list for each object you searched, all inside one outer list.
The keyword that starts every SOSL search. It holds the words you are looking for.
The error you get when a query goes wrong, like putting zero rows, or two, into one record.
Words added to a query so it only returns what the running user may see: objects, fields and records.

lessons.title: DML statements and Database methods
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, write SOSL, SOQL, and DML statements in Apex, and assess what they will return.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **DML** (data manipulation language) is how Apex changes records: `insert`, `update`, `upsert`, `delete`, `undelete` and `merge`. You can write a **DML statement**, like `insert accts;`. Or you can call a **Database method**, like `Database.insert(accts, false);`.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Mailing a stack of letters. A DML statement is all or nothing: one bad address and the whole stack comes back. A Database method with `false` is "send what you can": good letters go, bad ones come back with a note. Where it stops: either way, it's still one trip, one DML, for the whole stack.

cards.title: All or nothing
cards.body: A DML statement throws a `DmlException` on any failure, and none of the records are saved. Catch it with try/catch.

cards.title: Partial success
cards.body: Setting **allOrNone** to `false` lets good records save. You get one **SaveResult** per record, in the same order. Bad records don't throw an exception.

cards.title: upsert
cards.body: **upsert** inserts new records and updates existing ones in one call. It matches on `Id`, or on an **External ID** field you name: `upsert recs Order_Key__c;`. No match: insert. One match: update. Several matches: error.

cards.title: DML limits per transaction
items: **150** DML statements. Each `insert`, `update` or `Database` call counts once, however many records it has.
**10,000** records processed by DML in total.
Put records in a `List` and run **one** DML. Never one per record in a loop.

cards.title: Undo with a savepoint
cards.body: `Database.setSavepoint()` marks a point in the transaction. `Database.rollback(sp)` undoes every DML since that point. Use it when a later step fails and the earlier steps must be undone too.
`Database.insert(recs, false)` does **not** throw for bad records. Code that only uses try/catch will miss them. Always loop over the results and check `isSuccess()`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Statement = strict. Database with false = forgiving.** Bulk it up: one list, one DML.

terms.say: Apex commands that change records: insert, update, upsert, delete, undelete and merge.
The short way to change records, like `insert accts;`. If any record fails, none are saved and you get an error.
The method way to change records, like `Database.insert()`. It can let good records save while bad ones fail.
The error Apex throws when a DML statement fails, for example a required field is missing.
A true or false setting on Database methods. False means "save the good ones, report the bad ones".
A small report for one record after a Database insert or update. It says if it worked, and if not, why.
Insert or update in one step. If a matching record exists, update it. If not, create it.
A field you mark as an outside system's key, like an order number, so upsert can match records by it.
Marks a spot in the transaction. Later you can roll back to it and undo every change made after.

lessons.title: The save order of execution
lessons.objective: Describe the relationship between Apex transactions, the save order of execution, and the potential for recursion and/or cascading.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: When a record is saved, Salesforce runs a fixed list of steps: flows, triggers, rules, then the final save. This is the **order of execution**. It tells you which automation sees which value, and why some code runs twice.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: An airport. Check-in, security, boarding, takeoff, always in that order. Each step sees what the step before it did. Where it stops: some steps, like a workflow field update, send you back through security one more time.

cards.title: The save line (main steps)
items: 1. System validation, then **before-save flows**
2. **Before triggers**
3. Validation rules, then duplicate rules
4. Record saved, but not committed
5. **After triggers**
6. Assignment, auto-response and workflow rules
7. **After-save flows**
8. Roll-up summaries update the parent
9. **Commit**, then emails and async jobs

cards.title: Workflow loops back
cards.body: A **workflow field update** saves the record again. Before update and after update triggers run **one more time, and only once**. Custom validation rules, duplicate rules and flows don't run again.

cards.title: One transaction
cards.body: Everything in one save is one **transaction**. If an error isn't handled, the whole transaction **rolls back** and nothing is saved. Governor limits count across the whole transaction, for every trigger and flow in it.

cards.title: Cascading saves
cards.body: A trigger that updates another record starts that record's own save line, inside the same transaction. That's **cascading**. Roll-up summaries do it too: the parent goes through its own save.
Two triggers on the same object and event? Their order **isn't guaranteed**. Don't count on one running first. Use one trigger per object that calls a handler class in the order you choose.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Flow, trigger, check, save, trigger, rules, flow, roll-up, commit.** "Before" steps change the record. "After" steps react to it.

terms.say: The fixed list of steps Salesforce runs every time a record is saved. Same steps, same order, every time.
Record-triggered flows that run first, before the triggers, to quickly change the record being saved.
Apex triggers that run before the record is saved, after the before-save flows.
Apex triggers that run after the record is saved but before it's final. Now the record has an Id.
Record-triggered flows that run late in the save, after the triggers and workflow rules.
An old-style rule that changes a field after the save. It saves the record again, so update triggers run once more.
Everything that happens in one save, start to finish. It all succeeds together, or it is all undone together.
Undoes every change in the transaction, as if nothing was saved.
When one save causes another save, like a trigger updating a parent record. It all happens in one transaction.
The moment the changes become final in the database. Emails and async jobs only start after it.

lessons.title: Trigger basics and context variables
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, follow best practices to write Apex classes and triggers.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: An Apex **trigger** is code that runs by itself when records are inserted, updated, deleted or undeleted. Before triggers check or change records before they're saved. After triggers use the saved records, like their new Ids, to work on other records.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A doorbell camera. It wakes up by itself when someone arrives. A before trigger asks "are you allowed in?" An after trigger texts your family once you're inside. Where it stops: a trigger can wake up for 200 visitors at once, so always loop over a list.

cards.title: Trigger syntax
cards.body: Name, object, then the events in brackets. **Context variables** like `Trigger.isBefore` tell the code why it's running.

cards.title: Context variables
items: `Trigger.new`: new versions. Insert, update, undelete. Editable only in **before** triggers.
`Trigger.old`: old versions. Update and delete.
`Trigger.newMap`: Id to new record. Before update, after insert, after update, after undelete.
`Trigger.oldMap`: Id to old record. Update and delete.
`Trigger.operationType`: an enum value like `BEFORE_INSERT`.

cards.title: No Id before insert
cards.body: In **before insert**, new records have **no Id yet**, so there's no `Trigger.newMap`. Need the Id? Use **after insert**. Changing a field on `Trigger.new` in an after trigger throws a runtime error, because the record is already saved.

cards.title: Blocking a save
cards.body: `addError()` stops that record from saving and shows your message to the user.

cards.title: Keep triggers thin
cards.body: A trigger can't say `with sharing` or `without sharing`. Put that choice on the **handler class** the trigger calls. Keep triggers thin: one trigger per object, with the logic in classes.
`Trigger.new` in a delete trigger? It **isn't there**. Use `Trigger.old`. And `Trigger.old` doesn't exist in insert triggers, because there was no old record.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Before: fix the record. After: use its Id.** New for insert, old for delete, both for update.

terms.say: Apex code that runs by itself when records of one object are inserted, updated, deleted or undeleted.
Built-in values a trigger can read to learn what's happening: which records, which event, before or after.
The list of records being saved, with their new values. Only before triggers can change them.
The list of records as they were before this change. Only there for updates and deletes.
The new records in a map, looked up by Id. Not there in before insert, because new records have no Id yet.
The old versions of the records in a map, looked up by Id. Only there for updates and deletes.
Tells you the exact event as one value, like `BEFORE_INSERT` or `AFTER_UPDATE`. Handy with `switch`.
Marks a record as bad so it isn't saved, and shows your message to the user.
A normal Apex class that holds the trigger's real logic. The trigger just calls it.

lessons.title: Bulkified, limit-safe triggers
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, understand governor limits and their implications on Apex transactions.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Bulkified** code works the same for 1 record or 200. Triggers get records in batches, so code must handle lists. The two big rules: no SOQL in loops, and no DML in loops. Otherwise you hit **governor limits**, the hard caps Salesforce sets per transaction.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Shopping for a party. You don't drive to the store once per guest. You write one list, make one trip and carry it all home together. Where it stops: even one trip has a size limit, like 50,000 query rows.

cards.title: Bad: a query in a loop
cards.body: One query per Contact. With 200 Contacts, that's 200 queries, far past the limit of **100**.

cards.title: Good: collect, query once, map
cards.body: Collect Ids in a **Set**, run **one** query, then look up each parent in a **Map**.

cards.title: Limits that bite (per transaction)
items: **100** SOQL queries, or **200** in async Apex.
**150** DML statements.
**50,000** query rows and **10,000** DML rows.
**10,000 ms** of CPU time, or **60,000 ms** async.
Going over throws `LimitException`, which **can't be caught**.

cards.title: Check as you go
cards.body: The `Limits` class shows what you've used so far, like `Limits.getQueries()` against `Limits.getLimitQueries()`. It's handy in debug logs while you tune code.

cards.title: Recursion
cards.body: A trigger that updates its own object fires itself again. That's **recursion**. Apex stops it at a **trigger depth** of 16, but it burns limits long before that. Guard it with a `static Set<Id>` of records already handled.
One `static Boolean` "ran once" switch looks safe. But all chunks of 200 share one transaction, so it skips every chunk after the first. Track handled records by Id in a `static Set<Id>` instead.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Collect, query once, map, loop, DML once.** No SOQL or DML inside a `for` loop. Ever.

terms.say: Written to handle many records at once, using lists, so 200 records cost the same queries as one.
Hard caps Salesforce puts on each transaction, like 100 queries, so one org can't hog shared servers.
A collection with no repeats. Perfect for gathering Ids before one query.
A collection of pairs: a key, like an Id, and its value, like a record. You look things up by key.
The computer time your code uses. Apex gets 10,000 ms per normal transaction.
The error thrown when code goes over a governor limit. No catch block can stop it.
A built-in Apex class that tells you how much of each limit your code has used so far.
Code that ends up starting itself again, like a trigger whose update fires the same trigger.
How many triggers deep a chain of saves can go. Apex stops it at 16.

lessons.title: Exceptions and custom exceptions
lessons.objective: Implement exception handling in Apex, including custom exceptions as needed.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: An **exception** is Apex saying "something went wrong, I can't go on". If nothing catches it, the whole transaction rolls back and the user sees an error. **Exception handling** lets your code catch the problem and react.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A safety net under a trapeze. `try` is the act. `catch` is the net that grabs a fall. `finally` is cleaning the stage, fall or not. Where it stops: some falls go right through the net, like going over a governor limit.

cards.title: try, catch, finally
cards.body: Catch the most specific type first. The general `Exception` catches anything left, except limit errors. `finally` runs either way.

cards.title: Built-in exceptions to know
items: `DmlException`: an insert, update or other DML fails.
`QueryException`: a query into one record finds 0 or 2+ rows.
`NullPointerException`: you used a variable that is `null`.
`ListException`: a list index is out of bounds.
`SObjectException`: you read a field you didn't query.
`LimitException`: a governor limit was hit. Can't be caught.

cards.title: A custom exception
cards.body: A **custom exception** is a class that `extends Exception`. Its name must end in the word **Exception**. You get message constructors for free.

cards.title: Useful methods
cards.body: `getMessage()` gives the text. `getTypeName()` gives the exception type. `getLineNumber()` and `getStackTraceString()` help debugging. For DML, `getNumDml()` and `getDmlMessage(i)` say which records failed.

cards.title: Show errors to users
cards.body: In a trigger, `addError('message')` blocks that record and shows the message. In an Apex method called by a Lightning component, throw an `AuraHandledException` so the user sees your own message.
A custom exception named `StockError` won't compile. The class name must end in **Exception**. Also, `catch (Exception e)` does **not** catch a `LimitException`. Nothing does.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Try it, catch it, finally tidy it.** Name custom ones something-Exception. Limits can't be caught.

terms.say: Apex's way of saying "something went wrong here". It stops the code unless something catches it.
Writing code that catches errors and reacts calmly, instead of letting the whole thing crash.
The block of code you want to run that might fail. If it fails, Apex jumps to a matching catch.
The block that runs when a matching error happens in the try block. It's the safety net.
A block that always runs after try and catch, error or not. Good for cleaning up.
The error you get when saving, changing or deleting records fails.
The error you get when you use something that is empty (null), like asking for the length of no text.
Your own error type, made by extending `Exception`. Its name must end in "Exception".
Gives you the error's text, so you can log it or show it.
A special error for Apex called by Lightning components. Its message reaches the user.

lessons.title: Apex and Flow together
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, use declarative functionality and Apex together to automate business logic.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Flows are great, but some jobs need code, like complex math or heavy logic. You can write that one piece in Apex and let a flow call it as an **Apex action**. The flow stays the boss. Apex is a helper it calls by name.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A restaurant. The flow is the waiter who runs the order. Apex is a chef called in for one tricky dish. The waiter hands in a list of orders and gets a list of dishes back. Where it stops: the chef must return one dish per order, in the same order.

cards.title: An invocable method
cards.body: `@InvocableMethod` turns the method into an action in Flow Builder. The `label` is the name admins see.

cards.title: Invocable rules
items: Must be `static`, and `public` or `global`, in an **outer class**.
Only **one** invocable method per class.
At most **one** input parameter, and it's a list: flows send data in bulk.
Return a list with one result per input, in the **same order**.
Need many inputs or outputs? Use a wrapper class with `@InvocableVariable` fields.

cards.title: Who can call it
cards.body: An invocable method can be called from Flow, from the REST API, from other Apex and from **Agentforce agents** as an action. The running user needs access to the Apex class.

cards.title: Starting a flow from Apex
cards.body: Apex can run an autolaunched flow with `Flow.Interview`. Pass input variables in a map, then call `start()`.

cards.title: Choosing the mix
cards.body: Start with Flow when clicks can do the job. Add an Apex action for the hard part. Write a full **trigger** only when you need complex logic on many records, tight control of order, or work Flow can't do.
An invocable method that takes one `Id`, not a `List<Id>`, won't save. Flows send inputs in bulk, so the parameter must be a list. And you can't have two invocable methods in one class.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **One per class. List in, list out, same order.** The flow drives. Apex is the expert it calls.

terms.say: A step in a flow that runs an Apex method. Admins drag it in like any other flow element.
An annotation that lets flows, agents and the REST API call this Apex method as an action.
The friendly name admins see for the action in Flow Builder.
Belongs to the class itself, so it can run without creating an object first. Invocable methods must be static.
A top-level class, not a class written inside another class. Invocable methods must live in one.
An annotation on a field of a wrapper class, so a flow can pass that field in or get it back.
Salesforce AI assistants. They can use invocable Apex methods as actions to get work done.
An Apex class for running a flow from code. You create an interview, give it inputs, then start it.
The method that actually runs a flow interview you created in Apex.
Apex that runs by itself when records are saved. Pick it when logic is too complex for a flow.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between a before-save and an after-save record-triggered flow?
flashcards.back: Before-save (Fast Field Updates) only changes the record being saved, very fast. After-save (Actions and Related Records) can change other records, send emails and call Apex.

flashcards.front: Which flow type shows screens to a user?
flashcards.back: A screen flow. Record-triggered, schedule-triggered, platform event-triggered and autolaunched flows run with no screens.

flashcards.front: What happens to a record when it's submitted for approval?
flashcards.back: By default it's locked. Only approvers and admins can edit it until the approval process finishes.

flashcards.front: Should new automation use workflow rules or Process Builder?
flashcards.back: No. Both are legacy tools. Salesforce recommends building new automation in Flow.

flashcards.front: How do you declare a constant in Apex?
flashcards.back: Use `static final`, like `static final Integer MAX = 5;`. Set it once: where it's declared, or in a `static` block.

flashcards.front: What value does an Apex variable hold before you set it?
flashcards.back: `null`. That's true for every type, even `Integer` and `Boolean`.

flashcards.front: Does `==` care about case when comparing Strings?
flashcards.back: No. `'abc' == 'ABC'` is true. Use `equals()` for a case-sensitive check. Map keys and switch values do care about case.

flashcards.front: How long does a `static` variable keep its value?
flashcards.back: For one transaction. Everything in that transaction shares one copy. The next transaction starts fresh.

flashcards.front: What does `public` mean in Apex?
flashcards.back: Any Apex in the same namespace or package can use it. To reach code outside the package, or from SOAP API, use `global`.

flashcards.front: What access does a method get with no modifier?
flashcards.back: `private`: only code in the same class can call it.

flashcards.front: What must a class do when it implements an interface?
flashcards.back: Define every method the interface lists. If one is missing, the class won't compile.

flashcards.front: What does `virtual` let you do?
flashcards.back: Extend the class, and replace its `virtual` methods with `override`. Classes can't be extended without `virtual` or `abstract`.

flashcards.front: Which types can a `switch on` expression use?
flashcards.back: `Integer`, `Long`, `sObject`, `String` and `Enum`. `null` is a legal `when` value for all of them.

flashcards.front: Does an Apex `switch` need `break` statements?
flashcards.back: No. At most one `when` block runs, and Apex never falls through to the next block.

flashcards.front: Which loop always runs at least once?
flashcards.back: A `do-while` loop. It checks its condition after the body runs.

flashcards.front: Why use a SOQL for loop?
flashcards.back: It fetches rows in chunks of 200, so a big result doesn't sit in memory all at once. It still counts as one query.

flashcards.front: What happens if a query into one record finds no rows?
flashcards.back: Apex throws a `QueryException`. The same happens with more than one row. Put the query into a `List` to get an empty list instead.

flashcards.front: What does a SOSL query return in Apex?
flashcards.back: `List<List<SObject>>`: one inner list per object, in the order of the `RETURNING` clause.

flashcards.front: How do you get a custom parent's field in SOQL?
flashcards.back: Use the relationship name ending in `__r`, then a dot: `Warehouse__r.City__c`.

flashcards.front: What are the SOQL limits per transaction?
flashcards.back: 100 queries (200 async) and 50,000 rows in total. SOSL: 20 queries and 2,000 rows per query.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between `insert recs;` and `Database.insert(recs, false)`?
flashcards.back: The statement is all or nothing and throws a `DmlException`. The method with `false` saves the good records and returns a `SaveResult` for each one.

flashcards.front: How does `upsert` decide to insert or update?
flashcards.back: It matches on Id or an External ID. No match: insert. One match: update. More than one match: error.

flashcards.front: What's the DML statement limit?
flashcards.back: 150 DML statements per transaction, and 10,000 records processed by DML.

flashcards.front: How do you undo part of a transaction?
flashcards.back: Mark a point with `Database.setSavepoint()`, then call `Database.rollback(sp)` to undo every DML since that point.

flashcards.front: Which runs first: a before-save flow or a before trigger?
flashcards.back: The before-save flow. Then before triggers, then custom validation rules and duplicate rules.

flashcards.front: What runs again after a workflow field update?
flashcards.back: Before update and after update triggers, one more time only. Custom validation rules, duplicate rules and flows don't run again.

flashcards.front: Is the order of two triggers on the same object and event guaranteed?
flashcards.back: No. Use one trigger per object that calls handler logic in the order you choose.

flashcards.front: When are emails and queued async jobs started from a save?
flashcards.back: After the transaction commits. If it rolls back, they never happen.

flashcards.front: When can you change `Trigger.new`?
flashcards.back: Only in before triggers. In after triggers the records are saved, so changing them throws a runtime error.

flashcards.front: Why is there no `Trigger.newMap` in before insert?
flashcards.back: The new records don't have Ids yet. Use after insert when you need the Id.

flashcards.front: Which context variables exist in a delete trigger?
flashcards.back: `Trigger.old` and `Trigger.oldMap`. `Trigger.new` isn't available in delete triggers.

flashcards.front: How do you stop one record from saving in a trigger?
flashcards.back: Call `addError('message')` on it. The record isn't saved, and the user sees the message.

flashcards.front: What does bulkified mean?
flashcards.back: The code handles a whole batch of records with one query and one DML, not one per record. Triggers get up to 200 records at a time.

flashcards.front: Can you catch a `LimitException`?
flashcards.back: No. Going over a governor limit stops the transaction and rolls it back. No catch block can handle it.

flashcards.front: Why is a single `static Boolean` a weak recursion guard?
flashcards.back: All chunks of 200 share one transaction, so chunks after the first get skipped. Use a `static Set<Id>` of handled records.

flashcards.front: How do you create a custom exception?
flashcards.back: Write a class that extends `Exception`. Its name must end in "Exception", like `StockException`.

flashcards.front: When does a `finally` block run?
flashcards.back: Every time, after the try and any catch, whether or not an error happened.

flashcards.front: What does `getNumDml()` tell you?
flashcards.back: How many records failed in the `DmlException`. Use `getDmlMessage(i)` to read each failure's message.

flashcards.front: What are the rules for an `@InvocableMethod`?
flashcards.back: It's `static`, `public` or `global`, in an outer class. One per class. At most one input, a list, and a list out in the same order.

flashcards.front: Who can call an invocable method?
flashcards.back: Flow, the REST API, other Apex and Agentforce agents. The running user needs access to the Apex class.

flashcards.front: How do you run a flow from Apex?
flashcards.back: Create it with `Flow.Interview.createInterview(name, inputs)`, then call `start()`.

questions.q: A service team wants agents to walk through a guided returns form: enter the order number, pick a reason, then confirm. Which flow type fits?
options: Screen flow
Record-triggered flow
Schedule-triggered flow
Platform event-triggered flow
questions.explain: Only a screen flow shows screens to a person. The agent clicks through each step, so this is a screen flow.
wrong: It runs on a record save and has no screens.
It runs on a timer for a batch of records, with no user.
It runs when an event message arrives, with no user.

questions.q: Sales ops wants Opportunity Next Step filled with "Qualify" whenever a new Opportunity is saved with it blank. They want no code and the fastest option. What should the developer build?
options: An after-save record-triggered flow that updates the record
A schedule-triggered flow that fixes blanks each night
A before-save record-triggered flow (Fast Field Updates)
A new workflow rule with a field update action
questions.explain: Changing the record that's being saved is fastest before the save. A before-save flow sets the field with no extra save.
wrong: It works, but it saves the record a second time, which is slower.
Records stay blank until night, and it isn't on save.
Workflow rules are legacy; build new automation in Flow.

questions.q: Which two jobs can an after-save record-triggered flow do that a before-save flow can't? (Choose 2)
options: Create a follow-up Task record
Update a field on the record that started the flow
Check a condition with a Decision element
Send an email alert
Show a custom error message to the user
questions.explain: Before-save flows can only change the record being saved. Creating other records and calling actions like email alerts need the after-save option.
wrong: Both options can do this; it's what before-save flows are best at.
Both options can use Decision elements.
Before-save flows can show a custom error too.
questions.source: Trailhead: Record-Triggered Flows

questions.q: A manager must approve any Opportunity discount over 20% before the deal moves on. While it waits, sales reps must not be able to edit it. Which feature fits best?
options: A validation rule on the Discount field
An approval process with a manager approval step
A screen flow on the Opportunity page
A roll-up summary field on Account
questions.explain: An approval process routes a record to approvers and, by default, locks it while it waits. That covers both needs.
wrong: It can block a save, but it can't ask a manager to approve.
It guides a user, but it doesn't route or lock the record.
It adds up child values; it doesn't approve anything.
questions.source: Trailhead: Approve Records with Approval Processes

questions.q: What happens to a record by default when a user submits it for approval?
options: It's deleted until an approver accepts it
It's copied into a separate approval object
Its owner changes to the first approver
It's locked, so most users can't edit it
questions.explain: The default initial submission action locks the record. Only approvers and admins can change it while it's pending.
wrong: Records are never deleted by submitting them.
The record stays where it is; it isn't copied.
Ownership doesn't change when a record is submitted.
questions.source: Trailhead: Approve Records with Approval Processes

questions.q: An admin builds a record-triggered flow on Case. It runs when a record is created or updated, and is optimized for Fast Field Updates. The admin wants to add a step that creates a follow-up Task, but Create Records isn't offered. Why?
questions.code:
Flow: Case_Follow_Up (record-triggered)
Object: Case
Trigger: A record is created or updated
Optimize for: Fast Field Updates
Elements: Decision -> Assignment -> [Create Records not available]
options: Create Records is only offered when the flow runs on create only
Flows can't create Task records, because Task is an activity object
Fast Field Updates can change only the triggering record
Create Records needs a scheduled path before it can be used
questions.explain: A before-save flow (Fast Field Updates) can only change the triggering record. To create a Task, switch to Actions and Related Records, which runs after the save.
wrong: Create-only or create-and-update makes no difference here.
After-save flows create Tasks all the time.
Create Records works on the main path of an after-save flow.
questions.source: Trailhead: Record-Triggered Flows

questions.q: If an Opportunity is still open 3 days before its Close Date, the owner must get a reminder email. The team wants a no-code solution. What is the best approach?
options: An after-save flow with a scheduled path 3 days before Close Date
A before-save record-triggered flow with a Pause element before the email
A schedule-triggered flow set to run once, 3 days after today
An after-save flow path set to run asynchronously, right after the save
questions.explain: Scheduled paths run later, at a time based on a date field on the record. Only after-save record-triggered flows have them.
wrong: Before-save flows can't wait and can't send emails.
It runs once on a fixed date, not 3 days before each Close Date.
An async path runs right after the save, not days later.
questions.source: Trailhead: Record-Triggered Flows

questions.q: A team lead asks which tool to use for brand-new automation that used to be built with workflow rules or Process Builder. What does Salesforce recommend?
options: Build a new workflow rule, since it's simpler
Build a new process in Process Builder
Always write an Apex trigger instead
Build it in Flow, the recommended tool for new automation
questions.explain: Workflow rules and Process Builder are legacy tools. Salesforce recommends Flow for new declarative automation.
wrong: Workflow rules are legacy; new automation belongs in Flow.
Process Builder is legacy; new automation belongs in Flow.
Clicks come first; code is for what Flow can't do.
questions.source: Trailhead: Flow Builder Basics

questions.q: A company wants these automations with no code. Which two are a good fit for a record-triggered flow? (Choose 2)
options: Let a rep step through a guided return form with input fields
Set a Lead's Rating as soon as a web-to-lead form creates it
Recalculate a score on every Account each Sunday night
React to a platform event message sent by an ERP system
Create a renewal Opportunity when an Opportunity is Closed Won
questions.explain: Record-triggered flows run when a record is created, updated or deleted. Setting a field on create and creating a record on a stage change both start from a record save.
wrong: A guided form needs a screen flow.
A weekly run over many records is a schedule-triggered flow.
Event messages start a platform event-triggered flow.
questions.source: Trailhead: Record-Triggered Flows

questions.q: A developer builds an autolaunched flow with no trigger to recalculate commissions. Which of these can start it?
options: Only a user opening a Lightning record page
Apex code, another flow or a REST API call
Only a change to a record of its object
Only a set time each day, chosen in the flow
questions.explain: An autolaunched flow with no trigger doesn't start by itself. Something else launches it, such as Apex, a parent flow as a subflow, or the REST API.
wrong: Opening a page doesn't start a flow by itself.
That describes a record-triggered flow.
That describes a schedule-triggered flow.
questions.source: Trailhead: Flow Builder Basics

questions.q: A developer needs a class-wide value that can never change after it's set. Which declaration does that?
options: `public static Integer MAX_TRIES = 5;`
`public static final Integer MAX_TRIES = 5;`
`public const Integer MAX_TRIES = 5;`
`public static constant Integer MAX_TRIES = 5;`
questions.explain: Apex constants use `final`, which means "set once". `static final` makes one shared constant for the class.
wrong: Without `final`, any code can change it later.
`const` isn't how Apex declares constants.
`constant` isn't an Apex keyword.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Constants

questions.q: A class has a member variable `public Boolean isVip;`. A new object of the class is created and no code sets `isVip`. What does `isVip` hold?
options: `false`
`true`
It won't compile until a default value is given
`null`
questions.explain: Every Apex variable starts as `null` until you set it. That includes `Boolean`, which is why you should set a starting value yourself.
wrong: Apex has no automatic `false` default; it starts as `null`.
Nothing set it to `true`.
Declaring without a value is allowed.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Primitive Data Types

questions.q: A developer collects Account Ids from 200 Contacts to use in `WHERE Id IN :ids`. Many Contacts share an Account, and the Ids should not repeat. Which collection fits best?
options: `Set<Id>`
`List<Id>`
`Map<String, Id>`
questions.explain: A Set keeps only one copy of each value. So each Account Id appears once, which is perfect for an `IN` filter.
wrong: A List keeps duplicates.
A Map needs a key for each value; it's more than this needs.
`Id[]` is just another way to write a List, so it keeps duplicates.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Sets

questions.q: What does this code print?
options: `false`, then `false`
`true`, then `true`
`true`, then `false`
`false`, then `true`
questions.explain: In Apex, `==` on Strings ignores case, so the first line is true. `equals()` checks case too, so the second is false.
wrong: `==` on Strings ignores case, so the first is true.
`equals()` is case-sensitive, so the second is false.
It's the other way round: `==` ignores case and `equals()` doesn't.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Expression Operators

questions.q: Which two statements about `static` variables in Apex are true? (Choose 2)
options: One value is shared by every user in the org
The value is kept between two separate saves by the same user
All code in the same transaction shares one copy
A `static` variable declared in a trigger keeps its value from before insert to after insert
The value resets when the transaction ends
questions.explain: A static variable lives for one transaction and is shared by everything in it. It starts fresh in the next transaction.
wrong: Each transaction gets its own copy; it isn't org-wide.
Two saves are two transactions, so the value resets.
Declare it in a class instead; a static in a trigger doesn't carry over between contexts.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Static and Instance Methods, Variables, and Initialization Code

questions.q: This runs in one Execute Anonymous transaction. What does it print?
options: `Total 3, mine 1`
`Total 2, mine 1`
`Total 1, mine 1`
Nothing; an instance method can't change a `static` variable
questions.explain: `total` is static, so both objects share it: three calls make it 3. `mine` is an instance variable, and `b` called `add()` once.
wrong: Three calls to `add()` raise the shared total to 3, not 2.
The static total is shared across both objects, not kept per object.
Instance methods can read and change `static` variables.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Static and Instance Methods, Variables, and Initialization Code

questions.q: A developer adds this class to hold a query size. What happens when they save it?
options: It compiles, and the first call to `init()` sets the value for the class
It compiles, but a second call to `init()` throws an error at run time
It fails to compile; a `static final` can't be set in a normal method
It compiles, and `LIMIT_ROWS` resets to `null` after each call
questions.explain: A `static final` variable can be set only once: in its declaration or in a `static` initializer block. Setting it inside a normal method is a compile error.
wrong: The compiler rejects setting a `static final` inside a regular method.
It never gets to run; the class doesn't compile.
It doesn't compile, so nothing resets.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Constants

questions.q: Which data type should hold a money amount like 1234.56 when exact decimals matter?
options: `Integer`
`Decimal`
`Currency`
`Double`
questions.explain: `Decimal` stores exact decimal numbers, and Currency fields map to it. It's the safe choice for money.
wrong: It holds only whole numbers.
Apex has no `Currency` type; Currency fields map to `Decimal`.
It's a floating-point number, so tiny rounding errors can creep in.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Primitive Data Types

questions.q: A developer tracks stock counts by product code. What does this print?
options: `Keys 1, apple 7`
`Keys 2, apple 3`
Nothing; `put` throws an error for a key that already exists
`Keys 2, apple 7`
questions.explain: `Map` keys of type `String` are case-sensitive, so `'apple'` and `'Apple'` are two keys. Putting `'apple'` again replaces 3 with 7.
wrong: Map String keys care about case, so there are two keys.
A second `put` on the same key replaces the old value.
`put` on an existing key just replaces its value.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Maps

questions.q: What is `tags.size()` after this line runs?
questions.code: Set<String> tags = new Set<String>{'red', 'blue', 'red'};
options: It throws an error for the repeated value
questions.explain: A Set holds no repeats. The second `'red'` is ignored, leaving `'red'` and `'blue'`.
wrong: A Set ignores the duplicate `'red'`.
Two different values remain: `'red'` and `'blue'`.
Duplicates are simply skipped; no error is thrown.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Sets

questions.q: A method in an Apex class is declared with no access modifier. Which code can call it?
options: Only code inside the class that declares it
Any Apex class in the same namespace
Any Apex code, plus the SOAP API
The class and any class that extends it
questions.explain: With no modifier, a method is `private`. Only code inside the class that defines it can call it.
wrong: That's `public`, which you must write out.
That's `global`, which you must write out.
That's `protected`, which you must write out.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Access Modifiers

questions.q: An ISV sells a managed package. Subscribers must call a utility method from their own Apex code. Which declaration works?
options: A `public` class with a `public static` method
A `public` class that has a `global static` method
A `global` class with a `public static` method
A `global` class with a `global static` method
questions.explain: Code outside the package can only reach `global` members. A `global` method must also sit in a `global` class.
wrong: `public` only reaches code in the same namespace.
A `global` method needs a `global` class.
A `public` method stays hidden from other namespaces.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Access Modifiers

questions.q: A developer saves this interface and class. What happens?
options: It compiles, and `carrier()` returns `null` when called
It fails to compile, because `carrier()` isn't implemented
It compiles, but calling `carrier()` throws a runtime error
It compiles, because only one interface method is needed
questions.explain: A class that implements an interface must define every method in it. `Parcel` skips `carrier()`, so it won't compile.
wrong: Missing interface methods stop the class from compiling.
The class never compiles, so nothing runs.
Every method in the interface is required.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Interfaces

questions.q: Which two statements about the `protected` access modifier are true? (Choose 2)
options: Classes that extend the defining class can use the member
It's the default when no modifier is written
Inner classes of the defining class can use the member
It can be used on `static` methods and variables
It makes the member visible to the SOAP API
questions.explain: `protected` opens a member to inner classes and to subclasses. It works on instance members only.
wrong: The default is `private`.
`protected` is for instance methods and member variables only.
SOAP API access needs `global`.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Access Modifiers

questions.q: What does this code print?
options: `Hi`
`Hi!`
Nothing; it fails to compile because `g` is typed as `Greeter`
Nothing; it throws a runtime error because `super` can't be used in an override
questions.explain: The object is a `LoudGreeter`, so its `override` runs, even through a `Greeter` variable. `super.hello()` calls the parent version and adds `!`.
wrong: The overriding method runs, because the object is a `LoudGreeter`.

questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Extending a Class

questions.q: A developer tries to save these two classes. What happens?
options: It compiles, and `StrictRule.check()` returns `false`
It compiles, but `check()` returns `true` because the override is ignored
It compiles only after `StrictRule` is marked `global`
It fails, because `BaseRule` can't be extended
questions.explain: Apex classes are closed by default. A class must be `virtual` or `abstract` to be extended, and the method must be `virtual` to be overridden.
wrong: It can't compile until `BaseRule` and `check()` are made `virtual`.
The compiler rejects the class; nothing runs.
Access level isn't the problem; the parent class isn't extendable.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Extending a Class

questions.q: Card, invoice and voucher payments each have their own logic and share no code. A checkout class must call `pay(amount)` on any of them without knowing which type it has. What is the best design?
options: Define an interface with `pay()`, and have each class implement it
Write one class with a `switch` on a type `String` inside `pay()`
Make each payment class `global` so the checkout class can find `pay()`
Copy the same `pay()` method into each class with no shared type
questions.explain: An interface is a shared promise. Checkout calls `pay()` through the interface type, and each class supplies its own logic.
wrong: It works, but every new payment type means editing that one class.
`global` controls who can see code; it doesn't give a shared type.
Without a shared type, checkout can't call them the same way.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Interfaces

questions.q: Which statement about an `abstract` class is true?
